title: Knock Control System Error (Extended Diagnostic)
shortDescription: Knock control module reports a generic system error after extended self-test.
fullDescription: The PCM has flagged an issue with the knock sensor system associated with code P0324. The knock sensor is a piezoelectric microphone bolted to the engine block that listens for detonation. When the signal is implausible, the PCM falls back to a conservative ignition timing map, reducing power and fuel economy.
safetyImpact: Engine power may be reduced; long-term untreated detonation can damage pistons and head gaskets.

fixSteps.title: Locate Knock Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find the knock sensor on the engine block (usually under the intake manifold). Inspect for oil contamination or damage.

fixSteps.title: Check Mounting Torque
fixSteps.instruction: Knock sensors must be torqued to the manufacturer spec — too loose or too tight changes resonance and triggers a code.

fixSteps.title: Measure Sensor Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect and measure resistance across the sensor terminals — typically a few hundred kilohms or open depending on type.

fixSteps.title: Replace Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace with OEM sensor and re-torque to spec. Clear codes and road-test under load.

faq.q: Can I drive with a knock sensor code?
faq.a: Yes, but timing will be retarded and you may notice reduced power. Avoid heavy load until repaired.

faq.q: Why is the sensor under the intake?
faq.a: Many V-engines bury the knock sensors in the valley to keep them close to all cylinders. Replacement is labor intensive.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit (Extended)
shortDescription: CKP A signal missing or implausible during extended test.
fullDescription: The PCM uses the crankshaft position sensor to determine engine speed and reference timing. When the signal is missing or implausible, the engine may stall, fail to start, or run with degraded fuel and ignition control.
safetyImpact: A no-start or stall condition is possible — sudden stalls can be hazardous in traffic.

causes.cause: Wiring chafed or routed near plug wires

symptoms: Tachometer drops to zero while running

fixSteps.title: Inspect Sensor and Connector
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the crankshaft sensor and inspect for oil leaks, debris, and connector integrity.

fixSteps.title: Scope the Signal
fixSteps.instruction: Use an oscilloscope to capture the waveform during cranking. Look for missing teeth or ratty signal indicating reluctor or air-gap issues.

fixSteps.title: Measure Resistance / Voltage
fixSteps.instruction: VR sensors should read a specific resistance; Hall sensors should toggle between ~0 V and ~5 V. Compare to spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace with OEM part, set air gap if applicable, and clear codes. Verify with a road test.

faq.q: Will the car run with this code?
faq.a: It may, but no-start and stalling are common. Don't ignore intermittent CKP/CMP codes.

faq.q: Do I need to relearn after replacement?
faq.a: Many vehicles require a CKP variation relearn with a scan tool after replacement.

causes.cause: Wiring chafed or routed near plug wires

symptoms: Tachometer drops to zero while running

fixSteps.title: Inspect Sensor and Connector
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the camshaft sensor and inspect for oil leaks, debris, and connector integrity.

fixSteps.title: Scope the Signal
fixSteps.instruction: Use an oscilloscope to capture the waveform during cranking. Look for missing teeth or ratty signal indicating reluctor or air-gap issues.

fixSteps.title: Measure Resistance / Voltage
fixSteps.instruction: VR sensors should read a specific resistance; Hall sensors should toggle between ~0 V and ~5 V. Compare to spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace with OEM part, set air gap if applicable, and clear codes. Verify with a road test.

faq.q: Will the car run with this code?
faq.a: It may, but no-start and stalling are common. Don't ignore intermittent CKP/CMP codes.

faq.q: Do I need to relearn after replacement?
faq.a: Many vehicles require a CKP variation relearn with a scan tool after replacement.

title: Ignition Coil Primary/Secondary Circuit (Extended)
shortDescription: Generic ignition coil primary/secondary fault under extended test.
fullDescription: The PCM monitors the primary side of each coil for proper switching. A fault on this circuit means the affected cylinder's coil is not firing correctly, leading to a misfire and possible catalytic converter damage if ignored.
safetyImpact: Unburned fuel can overheat the catalytic converter; long-term operation risks expensive damage.

causes.cause: Worn spark plug increasing coil load
Carbon tracking on boot or coil tower
Open or shorted coil control wire

symptoms: Check Engine Light flashing or steady

fixSteps.title: Read Freeze-Frame
fixSteps.instruction: Connect an OBD-II scanner and review freeze-frame data for cylinder the affected misfire history and ignition coil parameters.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Coil and Boot
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the cylinder the affected ignition coil and inspect the coil body, primary connector, and rubber boot for cracks, carbon tracking, or oil contamination.

fixSteps.title: Swap Test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap the suspect coil with a known-good coil from another cylinder. Recheck codes — if the misfire moves with the coil, replace it.

fixSteps.title: Verify Wiring & PCM Driver
fixSteps.instruction: Back-probe the coil control wire with a noid light or oscilloscope to verify the PCM is firing the coil. Replace the coil or repair wiring as needed.

faq.q: Can I drive with a flashing CEL?
faq.a: No — a flashing light means active misfire that will damage the catalytic converter quickly. Get the vehicle towed if possible.

faq.q: Should I replace plugs at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. Worn plugs are the leading cause of premature coil failure.
